module_question.FY1: How does physics measure and explain the world, from protons to galaxies?
module_question.FY2: Where does our energy come from, and how does using it affect the environment?
module_question.FY3: How is energy transferred as heat and work, and how does it change matter?
module_question.FY4: How do forces change the motion of an object?
module_question.FY5: Why do objects rotate and oscillate, and how do waves travel?
module_question.FY6: How does electric current flow in a circuit and transfer energy?
module_question.FY7: How are electricity and magnetism linked, and what is light?
module_question.FY8: Why is the energy of an atom quantised, and where does radiation come from?

lesson.computed_note: Computed from a model for this site.
lesson.exercise_path: You do not need to do every exercise. Start with the core exercises: they practise the main points of the chapter. Not all core exercises are calculations: in some you give written reasoning, draw a graph or a force diagram, or interpret measurement data. Then compare your answer with the model solution. The other exercises of levels 1 and 2 are extra practice if you want more certainty, and level 3 is challenging application.
lesson.level_lead_1: One formula or one step of reasoning. Core exercises first, the rest is extra practice.
lesson.level_lead_2: Two steps, working with measured data, a unit conversion or rearranging a formula. Core exercises first, the rest is extra practice.
lesson.level_lead_3: Optional: application, two ideas together or a new situation where you reason for yourself.
lesson.check_howto: Type your answer and press Check. An answer is accepted when it differs from the model answer by at most $2\,\%$ or by one unit in the last significant figure, whichever is larger. If your answer is $2$–$5\,\%$ away, the feedback is Close: then check the rounding and the significant figures. The answer and the solution open once you have checked an answer of your own. The hints open in order. The answer is checked in your browser and nothing is saved.
lesson.exercises_pending: The exercises for this lesson are still being checked. They will appear here when the check is done.
lesson.notice_legacy: Prototype version: this lesson was published before the current review process and is waiting to be renewed. The content may still change.

inquiry.lead_tarkista: Finally, assess whether you have reached the chapter's goals. If an answer is wrong, you get a suggestion of what to review.

fy2-2.selite: Filled dot: source or calculation. Ring: estimate.
fy2-2.s_foton: calculated from the Planck constant for a wavelength of $550\,\text{nm}$.
fy2-2.s_sydan: estimate: in one beat the heart gives the blood about $1\,\text{J}$ of mechanical energy.
fy2-2.s_omena: estimate: lifting an apple of about $0.1\,\text{kg}$ up by one metre takes about $1\,\text{J}$.
fy2-2.s_luoti: order of magnitude given by manufacturers for a .22 LR cartridge, about $150\,\text{J}$.
fy2-2.s_tikku: estimate: the wooden stick and head of a match release about $1\,\text{kJ}$ as they burn.
fy2-2.s_paristo: calculated from the capacity $2.5\,\text{Ah}$ and voltage $1.5\,\text{V}$ given by the manufacturer.
fy2-2.s_puhelin: estimate: a typical smartphone battery, about $54\,\text{kJ}$.
fy2-2.s_banaani: estimate: according to nutrition tables about $380\,\text{kJ}$ per hundred grams, and the edible part is about $120\,\text{g}$.
fy2-2.s_suklaa: estimate: milk chocolate packaging typically states about $2200\,\text{kJ}$ per hundred grams.
fy2-2.s_ruoka: estimate: according to nutrition recommendations an adult needs about $8\text{–}11\,\text{MJ}$ of energy per day.
fy2-2.s_bensiini: table value: the heat of combustion of petrol is $43\,\text{MJ/kg}$ and its density $0.75\,\text{kg/}\textsf{l}$ (Statistics Finland), which gives about $32\,\text{MJ}$ per litre.
fy2-2.s_kaasu: calculated: the heat of combustion of liquefied petroleum gas is about $46\,\text{MJ/kg}$, and the cylinder holds $11\,\text{kg}$.
fy2-2.s_salama: estimate: an average lightning strike; the variation is large (about $1\text{–}5\,\text{GJ}$).
fy2-2.s_tnt: definition: one tonne of TNT is agreed to equal $4.184\,\text{GJ}$.
fy2-2.s_lento: estimate: about $50\,\text{t}$ of jet fuel, heat of combustion about $43\,\text{MJ/kg}$.
fy2-2.s_uraani: calculated: one fissioning nucleus releases about $3.2 \cdot 10^{-11}\,\text{J}$, and a kilogram has about $2.6 \cdot 10^{24}$ nuclei.
fy2-2.s_ol3: calculated: net electrical power $1600\,\text{MW}$ for one day (TVO).
fy2-2.s_sahkopaiva: calculated: Finland's total electricity consumption in 2023 (Statistics Finland) divided by $365$ days.
fy2-2.s_tankkeri: estimate: about $100\,000\,\text{t}$ of crude oil, heat of combustion about $42\,\text{MJ/kg}$.
fy2-2.s_aurinko_s: calculated from the intensity of sunlight $1361\,\text{W/m}^2$ and the cross-sectional area of the Earth (NASA).
fy2-2.s_sahkovuosi: Statistics Finland: Finland's total electricity consumption was $79.8\,\text{TWh}$ in 2023, converted to joules.
fy2-2.s_suomi: Statistics Finland: total energy consumption was $1.32$ million $\text{TJ}$ in 2023.
fy2-2.s_jaristys: estimate: energy released as waves, from the USGS relation between magnitude and energy.
fy2-2.s_ihmiskunta: Energy Institute: world energy consumption was about $620\,\text{EJ}$ in 2023.
fy2-2.n_aurinko_h: Sun to Earth in one hour
fy2-2.s_aurinko_h: calculated: the energy of sunlight per second multiplied by $3600$.
fy2-2.s_asteroidi: estimate: the energy of the impact linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs; the range is wide.
fy2-2.s_aurinko: Energy radiated by the Sun per second, $3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\,\text{J}$ (IAU nominal value).

practice.title: Challenge tasks
practice.eyebrow: {{code}} · at the end of the module
practice.description: {{code}} {{title}}: exercises to solve independently, model answers and marking guides for self-assessment.
practice.lead: In these tasks nobody tells you which formula to use. Decide yourself which phenomena and models belong to the situation, solve the task on paper and justify your solution, as in the matriculation examination.
practice.howto: Solve the task yourself first, on paper or on a computer. You may use a calculator, a data booklet and graphing software. Write out your reasoning, formulas, substitutions and answers with units.
practice.reveal: Show the model answer and marking
practice.reveal_hint: Open only when your own solution is ready.
practice.rubric_lead: Compare your solution with the model answer and, for each item, choose the points you think your solution earns. Part marks are possible, and any other physically correct method is accepted too.
practice.own_rubric_lead: For each item, choose the points you think your report earns.
practice.rubric_note: The points are your own estimate, not a checked grade. The marking is Ruukkilabra's own, written according to the features of a good matriculation examination answer, and it is not official marking by the Matriculation Examination Board (YTL).
practice.course_lead: Extended application tasks, like the tasks in Part 3 of the example exam. They are not real exam tasks. The model answers and marking guides open after your own solution.

criteria.graph_axes: The axes show the correct quantities and units, and the scales are evenly spaced.
criteria.graph_points: Each measurement is marked as a separate point in the right place.
criteria.graph_fit: The model is fitted to the points it suits, and the points have not been joined into a broken line.
criteria.graph_read: The slope or other quantity is read visibly from the graph, using two points on the line that are far apart.
criteria.equation: The starting equation is correct, and the quantity asked for is solved from it before the numbers are substituted.
criteria.calculation: The numerical values are substituted with their units, and the calculation is correct.
criteria.units_precision: The answer has the correct unit and a precision that matches the given data.
criteria.reasonableness: The reasonableness of the result has been assessed.
criteria.uncertainty: The uncertainty of the measurement has been estimated.
criteria.error_sources: The main sources of error are named, and it is explained how they affect the result.
criteria.assumptions: The assumption is named, and its effect on the result is justified.
criteria.conclusion: The conclusion answers the question and is based on the data.
criteria.fbd_object: The object is clearly chosen, and only the forces acting on it are drawn.
criteria.fbd_forces: Every force acting on the object is included, and there are no invented forces.
criteria.fbd_directions: Every force points in the physically correct direction.
criteria.fbd_representation: Each force arrow starts at a sensible point on the object, and each force has its own unambiguous name.
criteria.fbd_magnitudes: The arrow lengths are in the right proportion where the sizes are known, and forces are not mixed up with components, velocity or acceleration.
criteria.fbd_equations: The equations of motion come from the free-body diagram: the axes and the positive direction are chosen, and the signs are right.

mixer.title: Exam task mixer
mixer.description: Every exam-style task of the site in one place: filter by module, competency or task type, or pick three at random.
mixer.lead: Here are all the exam-style tasks of the site, from the modules' challenge tasks and the lessons of the review course. Each task shows which chapters' skills it uses.
mixer.howto: Choose a module, a competency or a task type, or pick three tasks at random as for an exam. Solve a task yourself first, then open the model answer and the scoring on its page.
mixer.none: No task matches your choices. Choose Show all.
mixer.course_lead: All exam-style tasks of the review lessons and the modules on one page, to filter or pick at random.

exam.title: Example exam
exam.description: {{code}} {{title}}: an example exam in three parts like a course exam, with selection rules, model answers and marking guides.
exam.lead: This is a practice exam like a course exam. Do it as a real exam: calmly, without looking at the model answers until you are done.
exam.rule_all: answer every item, at most {{max}} p.
exam.rule_choose: answer {{choose}} of {{n}} tasks. Each task is {{points}} p, the part gives at most {{max}} p.
exam.max: The maximum score is {{max}} p. Tasks worth {{offered}} p are offered, but under the selection rules at most {{max}} p count.
exam.howto: Write your solutions on paper or a computer. You may use a calculator, a data booklet and graphing software. Open the model answers only when the whole exam is done.
exam.course_lead: Take the example exam at the end of the course like a real course exam: you have 120 minutes, and it has multiple-choice items and tasks to choose from. The model answers and marking guides open after the exam.
exam.total_note: The page scores the multiple-choice items when you open their model answer. The other points are your own assessment. In the optional parts the best tasks count under the rules.
exam.revise: If a task went badly, go back to the chapters listed under Skills from chapters for that task.

booklets.lead: Printable A5 booklets: the theory and worked examples of each course in one book. Tasks, simulations and model solutions are online: every chapter starts with a QR code to its page.
booklets.print_1: Print as a booklet: paper A4, page size A5, double-sided. The printer orders the pages so that the folded sheets make a booklet.
booklets.print_2: Without a booklet mode, print two pages per sheet double-sided, cut the sheets in half and bind the left edge. The figures are in colour: velocity, acceleration and force are told apart by colour.

teacher.title: Tools
teacher.lead: Tools for the teacher: a classroom screen and grading the submissions on your own computer.
teacher.desc: Tools for the teacher: the classroom screen and the grading page.
teacher.grading_p: Ruukkilabra submissions are graded on your own computer with this separate page. It does not use the network, and no student data comes to Ruukkilabra. Choose EN at the top of the grading page to use it in English; the task statements stay in Finnish.
teacher.update_p: Download the newest version whenever it is updated. The points and the imported submissions stay in the browser when you open the new version in the same browser.
teacher.step_1: Make a Forms form for each group, with a name that starts with the group (e.g. FY3.2 lv 2026-27 Palauta ratkaisut), and add its link to the page {{returns}}.
teacher.step_2: Download the form's response folder (File responses) from Drive as a zip file.
teacher.step_3: Open the grading page in Chrome or Edge and choose Tuo tiedosto (Import file) → the zip.
teacher.step_4: Choose a task and grade its solutions one after another: the numbers 0 and 1 and the arrows ← → change the points, ↓ ↑ change the student.
teacher.step_5: Export the points as a CSV file and back up the group to the school's Drive.
teacher.shot_opiskelija: A student's module page after six weeks: the tasks done day by day and the student's own self-assessment chapter by chapter (Finnish view).
teacher.shot_opettaja-kooste: The grading page's summary: 30 made-up students over six weeks, the tasks done, the points and the self-assessment.
teacher.shot_opettaja-sormenjalki: Group's learning fingerprint: each student's self-assessment of the chapter's goals, statement by statement, by theme and chapter (made-up students).
teacher.shot_opettaja-arviointi: Grading one task at a time: the task, the student's answer and the points 0–1 with the arrow keys.

guide.title: How to learn physics
guide.lead: You learn physics by experimenting, thinking, calculating and talking things through. You don't need to understand everything straight away. What matters most is to try for yourself and to practise regularly.
guide.description: How to learn physics with Ruukkilabra: where to start, what to do when a problem won't budge, and five tips for studying physics.

steps.title: Explore and predict
steps.text: Start with the chapter's opening questions. Think about what you expect to happen and why. Try the simulations and compare what you observe with your predictions. Wrong predictions teach you something too.

steps.title: Read the theory thoughtfully
steps.text: Get to know the concepts, figures, graphs and formulas. Try to understand what they mean. Stop and ask yourself whether you could explain it in your own words.

steps.title: Work through the guided examples
steps.text: Try to solve the examples yourself. Use the step-by-step guidance and the hints. Think about why the solution goes the way it does.

steps.title: Practise with the basic exercises
steps.text: Start with the Level 1 exercises and the core exercises. Once the basics feel solid, move on to harder ones. You don't need to do every exercise at once.

guide.stuck_lead: Everyone runs into hard parts. Try one of these.
guide.stuck_note: There is no set order: pick what suits the situation. You can ask for help right away.

ways.title: Draw and sketch
ways.text: Draw a picture of the situation. What do you know? What do you need to find out?

ways.title: Go back to the theory or an example
ways.text: Reread the part you need, or look at how a similar guided example was solved.

ways.title: Try a hint
ways.text: If the task has hints, open one at a time and try to carry on yourself.

ways.title: Talk it through and ask for help
ways.text: Talk with a classmate, compare your solutions or ask your teacher. Say what you have already tried.

guide.retry_text: If you looked at the model solution, solve the problem again without it.

tips.title: Draw it out
tips.text: A picture or a diagram helps you understand the situation. Draw a force diagram, for example, or sketch a graph.

tips.title: Explain in your own words
tips.text: Think about why the phenomenon happens, what the formulas mean and what your result tells you.

tips.title: Do the calculations yourself
tips.text: You learn to calculate by calculating. Think about the physics principle first, and at the end check the units and whether the result makes sense.

tips.title: Study together
tips.text: Talk with a classmate, compare ways of solving problems and explain things to each other.

tips.title: Review regularly
tips.text: Go back to old problems and test yourself without the model solutions. Short, repeated practice sessions help you remember.

guide.closing: Physics is not just memorising formulas. The aim is to understand phenomena and learn to solve problems.
